_meta.batch: GDPR — Sprint R2.1 Claim Map & Falsification (draft; minting BLOCKED)
_meta.status: R2.1 complete for discovery set — dispositions assigned; no EP-CLM-* or EP-SRC-* reserved; HTML blocked; GDPR Publish Gate not open
_meta.exit_gate: Every batch_1=true row has testable proposition, locator, actor, condition, complete exception/qualification, falsifier, non-advisory planning consequence, and primary source candidate. Owner may now KEEP selection for R2.2 mint drafts only.

batch_1_summary.note: Count follows material truth after mandatory splits; not a template target. Owner may still drop keeps before mint.

candidates.proposition_candidate: The GDPR is Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016, CELEX 32016R0679.
candidates.condition: N/A — identity proposition
candidates.exception_or_qualification: None.
candidates.falsifier: Any statement that a different instrument number is the GDPR.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Citing Directive 95/46/EC as the currently applicable GDPR.
candidates.current_state: In force; applies from 25 May 2018 (see CAND-03).
candidates.planning_consequence: Correct instrument citation in entry planning references and vendor questionnaires.
candidates.disposition_reason: Stable identity proposition; required for citation units.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 entered into force on the twentieth day following its publication in the Official Journal (published 4 May 2016 → 24 May 2016).
candidates.condition: Publication in the OJ triggers the Art. 99(1) clock.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: None for the entry-into-force rule itself.
candidates.falsifier: Stating entry into force on 25 May 2018 (that is application, Art. 99(2)).
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Conflating entry into force with application date on a clock surface.
candidates.planning_consequence: Separates baseline-active status from future-phased regimes (e.g. AI Act Art. 113).
candidates.disposition_reason: Falsifiable calendar fact; prevents date conflation with CAND-03.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 applies from 25 May 2018.
candidates.condition: Application date fixed by Art. 99(2).
candidates.exception_or_qualification: None for the general application date.
candidates.falsifier: Presenting GDPR general application as a future phased deadline after 25 May 2018.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Homepage/clock treating GDPR like an upcoming enforcement phase.
candidates.planning_consequence: Entry plans treat GDPR as an already-active baseline, not a deferred phase.
candidates.disposition_reason: Core temporal state for non-EU entry sequencing.

candidates.actor: Controller or processor established in the Union
candidates.proposition_candidate: The GDPR applies to processing of personal data in the context of the activities of an establishment of a controller or a processor in the Union, regardless of whether the processing takes place in the Union.
candidates.condition: Processing in the context of Union-establishment activities.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Does not itself decide Art. 3(2) non-establishment cases (see CAND-05/06).
candidates.falsifier: Claiming establishment presence is irrelevant once servers are outside the EU.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Non-EU parent ignoring EU branch/entity processing context.
candidates.planning_consequence: EU entity/branch design changes GDPR exposure mapping.
candidates.disposition_reason: Primary territorial limb for established operators.

candidates.actor: Controller or processor not established in the Union
candidates.proposition_candidate: The GDPR applies to processing of personal data of data subjects who are in the Union by a controller or processor not established in the Union where the processing activities are related to the offering of goods or services to such data subjects in the Union, irrespective of whether a payment is required.
candidates.condition: Art. 3(2) applies; activities related to offering goods/services to data subjects in the Union.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Not a catch-all for any EU personal contact; limited to the offering-related processing activities test in Art. 3(2)(a).
candidates.falsifier: Any contact with an EU person triggers GDPR regardless of offering.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Passive informational site with no offering framed as automatic Art. 3(2)(a).
candidates.planning_consequence: Go-to-market, pricing, language, and shipping design are entry gates for non-EU companies.
candidates.disposition_reason: Material non-EU targeting limb.

candidates.actor: Controller or processor not established in the Union
candidates.proposition_candidate: The GDPR applies to processing of personal data of data subjects who are in the Union by a controller or processor not established in the Union where the processing activities are related to the monitoring of their behaviour as far as their behaviour takes place within the Union.
candidates.condition: Art. 3(2) applies; monitoring of behaviour taking place within the Union.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Limited to behaviour monitoring within the Union; not every analytics cookie worldwide.
candidates.falsifier: Equating any cookie use anywhere with Art. 3(2)(b).
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Global telemetry with no EU-behaviour monitoring framed as automatic Art. 3(2)(b).
candidates.planning_consequence: Tracking/analytics/profiling architecture must be mapped before EU launch.
candidates.disposition_reason: Material non-EU monitoring limb.

candidates.actor: Controller not established in the Union
candidates.proposition_candidate: The GDPR applies to processing by a controller not established in the Union but in a place where Member State law applies by virtue of public international law.
candidates.condition: Place where MS law applies by public international law.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Narrow factual category; not a general non-EU residual clause.
candidates.falsifier: Using Art. 3(3) as a residual catch-all for all non-EU controllers.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Diplomatic/mission edge cases treated as ordinary SaaS entry paths.
candidates.current_state: Currently applicable but rare for typical SaaS entry.
candidates.planning_consequence: Usually out of scope for standard non-EU SaaS entry maps.
candidates.disposition_reason: Low frequency for Wave-1 non-EU SaaS entry; revisit if a product context requires it.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Controller means the natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data; Union or Member State law may determine the controller or criteria for nomination.
candidates.condition: Determination of purposes and means.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Union/MS law may designate controller; joint determination → Art. 26.
candidates.falsifier: Equating hosting a database with automatic controllership.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Cloud vendor assumed controller solely because it stores data.
candidates.planning_consequence: Role map precedes contracts and transfer tools.
candidates.disposition_reason: Foundational role definition.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Processor means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which processes personal data on behalf of the controller.
candidates.condition: Processing on behalf of a controller.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: If the processor determines purposes and means, Art. 28(10) treats it as controller for that processing.
candidates.falsifier: Labeling every SaaS vendor a processor without on-behalf analysis.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Independent analytics company deciding purposes called processor.
candidates.planning_consequence: Vendor classification drives Art. 28 contract and sub-processor graph.
candidates.disposition_reason: Foundational role definition.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Where two or more controllers jointly determine purposes and means, they are joint controllers and must determine their respective responsibilities transparently by arrangement, unless and insofar as responsibilities are determined by Union or Member State law; the essence of the arrangement shall be made available to the data subject.
candidates.condition: Joint determination of purposes and means.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Arrangement not required to the extent responsibilities are determined by Union/MS law; data subject may exercise rights against each controller (Art. 26(3)).
candidates.falsifier: Omitting joint-controller analysis for marketplaces/partnerships that jointly set purposes.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Platform + merchant jointly deciding purposes with no arrangement essence.
candidates.planning_consequence: Partnership/marketplace entry needs responsibility allocation before launch.
candidates.disposition_reason: High-frequency multi-party entry pattern.

candidates.actor: Controller or processor not established in the Union (where Art. 3(2) applies)
candidates.proposition_candidate: Where Article 3(2) applies, the controller or the processor shall designate in writing a representative in the Union.
candidates.condition: Article 3(2) applies.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Qualified by Art. 27(2) — see CAND-11b.
candidates.falsifier: Stating a universal representative duty for every non-EU company regardless of Art. 3(2) and Art. 27(2).
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: US company with no Art. 3(2) nexus told it must appoint an EU representative.
candidates.planning_consequence: Non-EU entry structure must test representative requirement as a gate.
candidates.disposition_reason: Mandatory split: default duty only; exceptions in CAND-11b.

candidates.actor: Controller or processor otherwise in scope of Art. 27(1)
candidates.proposition_candidate: The Art. 27(1) designation obligation does not apply to (a) processing that is occasional, does not include on a large scale Art. 9(1) special categories or Art. 10 criminal-conviction data, and is unlikely to result in a risk to rights and freedoms, taking into account nature, context, scope and purposes; or (b) a public authority or body.
candidates.condition: Exception analysis under Art. 27(2)(a) or (b).
candidates.exception_or_qualification: This proposition is itself the qualification of CAND-11a; Art. 27(2)(a) is conjunctive (occasional + not large-scale special/criminal + unlikely risk).
candidates.falsifier: Treating any occasional processing as exempt without the full Art. 27(2)(a) conjunction.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Regular B2C offering mislabeled occasional to avoid representative.
candidates.planning_consequence: Representative gate cannot be closed without documenting Art. 27(2) analysis.
candidates.disposition_reason: Mandatory split companion; qualifies CAND-11a.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the Art. 6(1)(a)-(f) bases applies.
candidates.condition: At least one listed basis must apply to the processing.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Each basis has its own conditions (e.g. Art. 6(1)(f) balancing; Art. 6(1)(f) second subparagraph excludes public authorities performing their tasks). Art. 6(2)-(3) allow MS/Union adaptation for points (c) and (e). This batch keeps one structural gate — not six automatic per-basis claims.
candidates.falsifier: Asserting processing is lawful without identifying an Art. 6(1) basis.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Entry plan with data flows but no legal-basis matrix.
candidates.planning_consequence: Entry plans need a legal-basis map per material processing activity.
candidates.disposition_reason: One structural proposition; independent per-basis claims only if later decision utility requires (not auto-split to six).

candidates.proposition_candidate: Personal data shall be processed in accordance with the Art. 5(1) principles (lawfulness/fairness/transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality).
candidates.condition: Applies to personal data processing under the Regulation.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Art. 5(1)(b)/(e) contain purpose/storage accommodations for Art. 89(1) archiving/research/statistics with safeguards. Art. 23 restrictions are NOT treated here as a general qualifier of Art. 5(1) — any Art. 23 link requires a separate verified proposition.
candidates.falsifier: Collapsing all principles into a vague fairness slogan without the Art. 5(1) list.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Product collecting unbounded data with no minimisation analysis.
candidates.planning_consequence: Product data model and retention design constraints before EU launch.
candidates.disposition_reason: Split from accountability (13b); no Art. 23 general qualifier without separate claim.

candidates.proposition_candidate: The controller shall be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, Article 5(1) (accountability).
candidates.condition: Controller responsibility for Art. 5(1) compliance demonstration.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Distinct from Art. 5(1) principles list; overlaps operationally with Art. 24 but is a separate normative statement.
candidates.falsifier: Treating accountability as optional documentation culture rather than Art. 5(2) duty.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: No evidence pack / records to demonstrate principles compliance.
candidates.planning_consequence: Governance evidence pack is an entry deliverable, not post-hoc.
candidates.disposition_reason: Mandatory conceptual split from principles.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Processing of special categories of personal data is prohibited unless an Art. 9(2) exception applies.
candidates.condition: Art. 9(1) special categories in scope.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Extensive Art. 9(2) exceptions — must not publish bare prohibition without exception architecture.
candidates.falsifier: Bare prohibition without exception map.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Health/biometric feature with no Art. 9 path.
candidates.planning_consequence: Sector-sensitive products need Art. 9 path before launch.
candidates.disposition_reason: Material for some products but not universal Wave-1 SaaS entry; mint when product context requires.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Taking into account nature, scope, context, purposes and risks, the controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure and be able to demonstrate that processing is performed in accordance with the GDPR, review/update where necessary, and where proportionate implement appropriate data-protection policies.
candidates.condition: Risk-based appropriateness relative to processing.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Art. 24(3): approved codes/certification may be an element of demonstration — not a substitute for the duty.
candidates.falsifier: Claiming policies alone without risk-appropriate measures.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Policy PDF with no operational controls.
candidates.planning_consequence: Security/governance design is part of entry readiness.
candidates.disposition_reason: Core accountability architecture for entry.

candidates.proposition_candidate: The controller shall implement data protection by design and by default: appropriate measures at determination of means and during processing to implement principles effectively, and by default only personal data necessary for each specific purpose (amount, extent, storage, accessibility).
candidates.condition: Applies at means determination and during processing; default necessity.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Risk-based / state of the art / cost factors in Art. 25(1); certification may be an element under Art. 25(3).
candidates.falsifier: Bolting privacy features after EU launch as sufficient by-design compliance.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Public-by-default profile settings for EU users.
candidates.planning_consequence: Product architecture decisions before EU market activation.
candidates.disposition_reason: High information-gain for product entry design.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Where processing is carried out on behalf of a controller, the controller shall use only processors providing sufficient guarantees; processing shall be governed by a contract or other legal act with Art. 28(3) mandated content; sub-processors require prior authorisation and flow-down (Art. 28(2),(4)).
candidates.condition: Processing on behalf of a controller.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Art. 28(10): processor determining purposes/means is controller for that processing. Codes/cert may support guarantees (Art. 28(5)).
candidates.falsifier: Using a vendor without Art. 28 terms because TOR were signed.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Sub-processor added with no controller authorisation path.
candidates.planning_consequence: Vendor and sub-processor graph is a pre-entry procurement gate.
candidates.disposition_reason: Central vendor-stack decision utility.

candidates.actor: Controller (and where applicable representative); processor (and where applicable representative)
candidates.proposition_candidate: Each controller shall maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility containing Art. 30(1)(a)-(g); each processor shall maintain a record of categories of processing carried out on behalf of a controller containing Art. 30(2)(a)-(d); records shall be in writing including electronic form and made available to the SA on request (Art. 30(3)-(4)).
candidates.condition: Controller/processor obligations under Art. 30(1)-(2).
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Qualified by Art. 30(5) — see CAND-18b.
candidates.falsifier: Asserting no RoPA needed for any SME without Art. 30(5) analysis.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Scaling SaaS with no processing record.
candidates.planning_consequence: RoPA is an entry planning deliverable.
candidates.disposition_reason: Mandatory split: duty vs conditional exemption.

candidates.actor: Enterprise or organisation employing fewer than 250 persons
candidates.proposition_candidate: The Art. 30(1)-(2) record obligations do not apply to an enterprise or organisation employing fewer than 250 persons unless the processing is likely to result in a risk to rights and freedoms of data subjects, the processing is not occasional, or the processing includes Art. 9(1) special categories or Art. 10 criminal-conviction data.
candidates.condition: Fewer than 250 persons AND none of the three restoring conditions.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: This is the qualification of CAND-18a; the three unless-conditions restore the duty even below 250.
candidates.falsifier: Fewer than 250 employees automatically means no RoPA.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Non-occasional B2C processing at headcount 200 with no records.
candidates.planning_consequence: Headcount alone does not close the RoPA gate.
candidates.disposition_reason: Mandatory split companion for Art. 30(5).

candidates.proposition_candidate: Taking into account state of the art, implementation costs, nature/scope/context/purposes and risk, the controller and the processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including as appropriate the Art. 32(1)(a)-(d) measures; risk assessment shall consider Art. 32(2) breach-type risks.
candidates.condition: Risk-appropriate security relative to processing.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Codes/certification may be an element of demonstration (Art. 32(3)).
candidates.falsifier: Checklist encryption alone equals Art. 32 compliance regardless of risk.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: No resilience/restore testing for critical EU customer data.
candidates.planning_consequence: Security architecture and vendor diligence before EU ops.
candidates.disposition_reason: Core security gate for entry.

candidates.proposition_candidate: In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the competent supervisory authority under Article 55; if not notified within 72 hours, the notification shall be accompanied by reasons for the delay.
candidates.condition: Personal data breach; controller awareness.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Qualified by the Art. 33(1) risk threshold — see CAND-20b.
candidates.falsifier: 72 hours as an absolute deadline with no undue-delay/feasibility reading and no risk threshold.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: No incident playbook for EU-connected personal data.
candidates.planning_consequence: Incident response design is a pre-entry operational gate.
candidates.disposition_reason: Default notify duty; threshold split to CAND-20b.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Notification to the supervisory authority under Art. 33(1) is not required where the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
candidates.condition: Breach assessed as unlikely to result in such a risk.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: This qualifies CAND-20a; documentation duty in Art. 33(5) still applies to breaches.
candidates.falsifier: Silent non-notification without a documented unlikely-risk assessment.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Credential stuffing on EU accounts ignored as unlikely without analysis.
candidates.planning_consequence: IR playbooks must include risk-threshold assessment, not only a 72h timer.
candidates.disposition_reason: Explicit unless-qualification required before mint.

candidates.proposition_candidate: When a personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall communicate the breach to the data subject without undue delay, in clear and plain language, including at least the information in Art. 33(3)(b)-(d).
candidates.condition: Likely high risk to rights and freedoms.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Qualified by Art. 34(3) — see CAND-21b.
candidates.falsifier: Equating every Art. 33 SA notification with mandatory data-subject communication.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Encrypted-at-rest breach notified to SA and mass-emailed to users without high-risk analysis.
candidates.planning_consequence: Comms/IR plan distinguishes SA notify vs data-subject communicate.
candidates.disposition_reason: Kept in batch-1 with mandatory Art. 34(3) companion.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Communication to the data subject under Art. 34(1) is not required if (a) appropriate technical and organisational protection measures were applied to the affected data (in particular rendering them unintelligible to unauthorised persons, such as encryption); or (b) subsequent measures ensure the high risk is no longer likely to materialise; or (c) it would involve disproportionate effort, in which case there shall instead be a public communication or similar equally effective measure.
candidates.condition: One of Art. 34(3)(a)-(c) met.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: This qualifies CAND-21a; SA may still require communication (Art. 34(4)).
candidates.falsifier: Disproportionate effort used to avoid any effective communication.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: No public notice after claiming disproportionate effort.
candidates.planning_consequence: IR playbooks must encode Art. 34(3) branches explicitly.
candidates.disposition_reason: Art. 34(3) exceptions completed for batch-1.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Where a type of processing — in particular using new technologies — and taking into account nature, scope, context and purposes, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall carry out a DPIA prior to processing. Art. 35(3) lists cases in which a DPIA is in particular required (systematic extensive evaluation/profiling with legal/similarly significant effects; large-scale Art. 9/10 data; large-scale systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area).
candidates.condition: Likely high risk (primary trigger). New technologies are an indicator context, not an automatic standalone trigger.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Art. 35(3) are structured indicators of when DPIA is in particular required. SA lists under Art. 35(4)-(5) may add/exclude kinds. Art. 35(10) limited carve-out where legal-basis impact assessment already covers processing under Art. 6(1)(c)/(e) unless MS require otherwise.
candidates.falsifier: New technology automatically requires DPIA regardless of high-risk analysis.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Low-risk encryption library upgrade labeled DPIA-mandatory solely as new tech.
candidates.planning_consequence: High-risk feature design triggers DPIA before EU activation.
candidates.disposition_reason: High-risk centred; 35(3) as indicators not synonym of new-tech rule.

candidates.proposition_candidate: The controller and the processor shall designate a data protection officer where (a) processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except courts acting in their judicial capacity; or (b) core activities consist of processing operations that require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale; or (c) core activities consist of large-scale processing of Art. 9 special categories or Art. 10 criminal-conviction data.
candidates.condition: At least one of Art. 37(1)(a), (b), or (c) is met.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: There is no universal default DPO duty. Art. 37(4) permits or requires designation in other cases under Union/MS law — out of batch-1 as a separate optional path. Group/public-authority single-DPO logistics in Art. 37(2)-(3) are operational detail, not a substitute trigger.
candidates.falsifier: Every company processing EU personal data must appoint a DPO.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Early-stage B2B SaaS with no 37(1) trigger told DPO is mandatory.
candidates.planning_consequence: Org design tests 37(1) triggers — does not assume a default DPO.
candidates.disposition_reason: Trigger model (a)/(b)/(c) — not default-then-exception.

candidates.proposition_candidate: Any transfer of personal data which are undergoing processing or are intended for processing after transfer to a third country or international organisation shall take place only if the Chapter V conditions are complied with by the controller and processor (including onward transfers), applied so that the level of protection is not undermined.
candidates.condition: Transfer to third country or international organisation.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Art. 44 is the Chapter V gate. Pathways below are hierarchical: adequacy (Art. 45) → appropriate safeguards (Art. 46) → derogations (Art. 49) — not four equal alternatives.
candidates.falsifier: Treating SCCs, adequacy, and Art. 49 derogations as interchangeable equal options.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Using Art. 49 consent as the primary standing transfer tool for routine US hosting.
candidates.planning_consequence: Transfer architecture must be designed before freezing cloud regions/vendors.
candidates.disposition_reason: Chapter V hierarchy root.

candidates.actor: Controller/processor relying on adequacy; Commission decides
candidates.proposition_candidate: A transfer may take place where the Commission has decided that the third country, territory, specified sector, or international organisation ensures an adequate level of protection; such a transfer shall not require any specific authorisation. The Commission publishes the list of adequacy decisions; decisions are subject to periodic review and may be amended, suspended or repealed.
candidates.condition: Valid Commission adequacy decision covering the destination.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: This claim is about the **adequacy mechanism**, not a snapshot of which countries are currently adequate. A live country-list proposition is deferred (see CAND-25-DYNAMIC) because it requires Commission implementing acts + separate freshness contract.
candidates.falsifier: Publishing a static country list inside the Regulation claim as if Art. 45 itself enumerates countries.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Hard-coding adequacy countries in claims.json without Commission source pinning.
candidates.current_state: Mechanism currently applicable; country set is time-varying.
candidates.planning_consequence: Entry plans may use adequacy where a valid decision exists; must re-check Commission list under freshness rules.
candidates.disposition_reason: Mechanism only; dynamic country inventory deferred.

candidates.provision_locator: Commission adequacy implementing acts / Art. 45(8) list
candidates.proposition_candidate: DEFERRED — candidate for a future Commission-sourced claim stating the then-current set of adequate destinations.
candidates.condition: Would require pinned Commission decision IDs + retrieved_at + freshness trigger.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Cannot be supported by GDPR-SRC-CAND-01 alone.
candidates.falsifier: N/A until drafted.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: N/A
candidates.planning_consequence: Country/region selection monitoring.
candidates.primary_source_candidate: requires Commission Tier-1/2 pin at mint time
candidates.disposition_reason: Dynamic inventory needs separate source + freshness contract; not Regulation-text stable.

candidates.proposition_candidate: In the absence of an Art. 45(3) adequacy decision, a controller or processor may transfer personal data to a third country or international organisation only if appropriate safeguards are provided and enforceable data-subject rights and effective legal remedies are available; Art. 46(2) lists safeguards usable without specific SA authorisation (including SCCs and BCRs among others).
candidates.condition: No applicable adequacy decision; safeguards + enforceable rights/remedies.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Hierarchical position: only after Art. 44 gate and absence of Art. 45 adequacy. Art. 46(3) authorised mechanisms exist but are not expanded in batch-1.
candidates.falsifier: Using SCCs where an adequacy decision already covers the transfer without noting hierarchy.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: No transfer tool identified for US subprocessors.
candidates.planning_consequence: Contract/SCC/BCR design before vendor freeze.
candidates.disposition_reason: Safeguards pathway in Chapter V hierarchy.

candidates.proposition_candidate: In the absence of an adequacy decision and of appropriate safeguards, a transfer or set of transfers may take place only under one of the specific Art. 49(1) conditions (derogations for specific situations).
candidates.condition: No adequacy and no Art. 46 appropriate safeguards; a listed derogation applies.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Art. 49 is exceptional in the Chapter V hierarchy — not a primary standing transfer architecture for repetitive/systematic transfers. Exact Art. 49(1) points and the second subparagraph limits must be respected at mint wording.
candidates.falsifier: Consent under Art. 49 as the default transfer strategy for ongoing cloud hosting.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Production US region justified only by blanket Art. 49 consent.
candidates.planning_consequence: Entry plans must not treat Art. 49 as the default transfer design.
candidates.disposition_reason: Derogations kept but marked exceptional in hierarchy.

candidates.proposition_candidate: When deciding whether to impose an administrative fine and its amount, the SA shall give due regard to the Art. 83(2) criteria. Infringements listed in Art. 83(4) are subject to fines up to EUR 10 million or, for an undertaking, up to 2% of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. Infringements listed in Art. 83(5) are subject to fines up to EUR 20 million or, for an undertaking, up to 4% of such turnover, whichever is higher.
candidates.condition: SA fining decision under Art. 83; undertaking turnover test where applicable.
candidates.exception_or_qualification: Art. 83(1) effective/proportionate/dissuasive; Art. 83(3) multiple infringements cap; Art. 83(7) MS rules for public bodies; not scare-copy — tiers depend on which provisions are infringed.
candidates.falsifier: Reducing Art. 83 to a single maximum number without tiers or criteria.
candidates.counterexample_or_failure_case: Marketing page claiming automatic 4% fine for any GDPR issue.
candidates.planning_consequence: Risk register and board framing use tier structure and criteria — not a single scare figure.
candidates.disposition_reason: Criteria + two-tier structure kept visible; no scare-copy reduction.

candidates.proposition_candidate: REJECTED AS BATCH-1 UNIT — supervisory/enforcement architecture is too broad as a single proposition (establishment of SAs, competence, one-stop-shop, powers).
candidates.condition: N/A
